statement: Last month, $40\%$ of the members of a chess club were girls. Then $10$ boys joined the club and nobody left, and now $30\%$ of the members are girls. How many girls must join the club now so that exactly half of the members are girls?

choices.misconception: I used last month's $18$ boys instead of the $28$ boys there are now, and found $18 - 12 = 6$.
I took half of the $40$ members, which is $20$, and subtracted the $12$ girls. But the new girls make the club bigger, so half is no longer $20$.
I worked out that there are $28$ boys now and gave that as the number of girls who must join, forgetting the $12$ girls already in the club.
I wrote $0.4N = 0.3N + 10$, which gave $N = 100$ with $40$ girls and $70$ boys, so I said $70 - 40 = 30$ girls must join. The $10$ belongs inside: $0.3(N + 10)$.

hints: The number of girls did not change when the boys joined.
If the club had $N$ members last month, then the girls give $0.4N = 0.3(N + 10)$.
So $N = 30$: there were $12$ girls and $18$ boys, and now there are $12$ girls and $28$ boys. Exactly half are girls when the girls equal the boys.

solutions.reliable: Let $N$ be last month's number of members. The girls did not change, so $0.4N = 0.3(N + 10)$, which gives $0.1N = 3$ and $N = 30$. There were $12$ girls and $18$ boys; now there are $12$ girls and $28$ boys. Exactly half the members are girls when there are as many girls as boys, so $28 - 12 = 16$ girls must join. Check: then there are $28$ girls out of $56$ members, which is one half.
solutions.elegant: The same girls were $\frac{4}{10}$ of the old club and are $\frac{3}{10}$ of the new club, so the new club is $\frac43$ as big as the old one. The extra $\frac13$ of the old club is the $10$ boys, so the old club had $30$ members: $12$ girls and $18$ boys. Now there are $28$ boys, so $16$ more girls are needed.
